data.title: Private equity has been buying up hospice centers - with striking consequences
data.description:
By Jessica Hall

Medicare costs are higher and patients stay longer at hospice providers owned by private-equity firms, new research has found

Hospice provides care to people who are not expected to live longer than six months.

Hospice - providing care in the final days and weeks of a person's life - may not conjure up images of Wall Street, mergers and acquisitions, or big profit margins, but that's exactly what the $30 billion industry has become.

About 1.8 million Americans use hospice services each year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. There are more than 5,800 hospice agencies in the U.S., three-quarters of which are for-profit entities, according to the CDC.

When a private-equity firm buys a hospice-care provider, costs jump, length of stay increases and the patient mix changes, a new study has found. In some cases, questions arose about whether patients were appropriately enrolled in hospice care in the first place, the researchers said.

Hospice provides care for people with terminal illnesses who have a prognosis of six months or less to live. The goal is to manage pain and symptoms, rather than curing the illness, in the patient's final months, weeks or days before death. For people 65 and older, Medicare pays for hospice services. For routine hospice care - which is provided in the home - Medicare pays $225 a day for the first two months and $177 per day thereafter.

However, Medicare spending on hospice care rose 5.9% following a private-equity acquisition, as the average length of stay increased by 6.3 days, according to the federally funded study published in the journal Health Affairs.

"The extent and magnitude of our findings surprised us," said Sneha Kannan, the lead author of the study and an assistant professor at the University of Pittsburgh. "We showed that acquisitions result in higher costs and increased length of stay."

The U.S. hospice market was about $31.2 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $45.3 billion by 2033, growing at a compound annual growth rate of 4.8% from 2026 to 2033, according to Grand View Research.

In the study, the researchers compared 191 for-profit hospices acquired by private-equity firms between 2018 and 2022 with 1,305 similar for-profit hospices. After a private-equity acquisition, Medicare paid $993 more per hospice stay compared with comparable hospices. That's above the average baseline charge of $16,922.

In addition to the longer length of stay under hospice care, the patient profile changed to less medically needy - patients who need less hands-on care - and some patients also even exited hospice alive, the study found. That raised questions about whether they were appropriately enrolled in hospice in the first place, the researchers said.

"There may be inappropriate enrollment going on. Patients may have more than six months to live, which goes against the idea of hospice as end-of-life care," Kannan said. "In most care settings, a patient dies and that's not a good thing. But in hospice, the purpose is to care for them at the end of life."

The study also found that patients with dementia were admitted more often, suggesting that the private-equity hospices may have shifted toward patients who need less daily care than other patients, such as cancer patients who need active pain management. Having less needy patients is more profitable under Medicare's current method of payment, which pays a flat daily rate no matter the patient's diagnosis.

"It's possible it's the selection of patients," Kannan said. "It could be inappropriate enrollment."

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and the National Alliance for Care at Home, a hospice industry trade group, did not respond to requests for comment.

Medicare pays a set dollar amount per day regardless of the number of visits a patient gets or whether the care is provided by nurses, aides or social workers. The U.S. Government Accountability Office recently recommended that the payment method for hospice be revamped to pay for the number of patient visits rather than the number of days a patient spends in hospice.

Nonprofit hospice agencies have an annual profit margin of about 5% to 6%, while for-profit public or private-equity hospice firms sometimes have profit margins as high as 18% to 22%, according to a report by the University of Pennsylvania's Leonard Davis Institute of Health Economics.

The "hospice benefit is a rich benefit that can be quite profitable based on it largely being based on 'trust me,' in that you are given a daily rate regardless of visits, etc., and certain diagnoses with long lengths of stay are quite profitable. So [private equity] sees it as money maker," said Joan Teno, an adjunct professor of health services, policy and practice at Brown University and an expert on hospice.

Private equity "is based on quick turnover - some of the deals are just packaging hospices with high rates of live discharge, not making visits in the last days of life, and reselling. It is not improving the quality of care," Teno said.

The hospice industry has grown, in part due to the aging U.S. population. Medicare spending on hospice care nearly doubled from $15.5 billion in 2015 to $27.5 billion in 2024, according to MedPAC, the independent agency that advises Congress on Medicare issues. Yet the number of Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in the hospice grew at a slower rate of 32% - from 1.4 million in 2015 to 1.8 million in 2024, MedPAC found.

"Hospice is one of the most brilliant innovations of 20th-century healthcare. We watched as problems developed over the decades, and the crisis was utterly predictable and now has come to pass," said Ira Byock, a palliative-care physician, the author of several books on hospice and an emeritus professor at the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth.

The hospice industry has come under increased scrutiny in the past few years. CMS last week extended for an additional six months a national moratorium on hospice-provider enrollment in Medicare in an effort to combat fraud.

One of the biggest problems with hospice is the lack of explicit standards for key quality-of-care metrics such as appropriate caseloads, response time for emergencies, or even protocols on how to handle emergencies such as a patient with extreme pain or seizures, Byock said.

"Consumers have no power. For the most part, it's let the 'die-er' beware," Byock said. "Ownership shouldn't matter. What should matter is demonstrable levels of quality."

-Jessica Hall

data.title: 'Nvidia's turmoil has me spooked': Is it time to sell my stocks and buy real estate?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

If you are tempted to ditch stocks for property or CDs, take a deep breath before making any sudden moves

Quentin Fottrell: "I'm not convinced a spooked investor is the one most likely to make a smart move."

Investors are nervous. Again. You're not the only one spooked.

A Moneyist reader nearing retirement shared his fears: "With the market dropping so sharply, is this a good time to move some money out of investments in the S&P 500 SPX and consider other opportunities? I'm in my late 60s. Nvidia's turmoil has me spooked, so I'm looking at a couple of options."

"Real estate here in Florida seems to be presenting some interesting opportunities, with plenty of inventory and sellers who appear more willing to negotiate," he wrote. "Another possibility is moving some money into CDs, which are currently offering much more attractive interest rates."

It's a common knee-jerk reaction, and he may be overreacting. A drop isn't a crash, even when it feels like one, although we are now heading towards correction territory. The market fell sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic, and again after President Trump announced a trade war with multiple countries, including China. Both times, it recovered. And, yes, it's falling again this week amid Nvidia's woes.

The stock market regularly shows its teeth. It's the nature of the beast.

Still, I'm not convinced a spooked investor is the one most likely to make a smart move. It never ceases to amaze me how quickly people panic when the market turns south. But the market regularly shows its teeth. It's the nature of the beast.

The latest roar came from Nvidia (NVDA). CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after admitting he had been unfaithful to his wife amid reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly suspect of ties to Chinese intelligence. He also reportedly had relationships with two other Nvidia employees. U.S. regulators are clamping down on a loophole that allowed the sale of AI chips to China and other countries.

After the Nvidia scandal broke, Bernstein senior semiconductor analyst Stacy Rasgon cut his rating on Nvidia's stock to "market perform" from "outperform" and halved his price target to $200 a share. Oppenheimer analyst Rick Schafer cut the stock to "perform" from "outperform" and removed his price target.

Among their concerns: dependence on a single charismatic CEO, increased competition in AI chips and wider fears of an AI bubble. After Nvidia's earnings were released on Tuesday afternoon, you better believe that analysts have questions. Take the long view, even if 2026 suddenly looks like a glum year for equities-and go play Grand Theft Auto VI (TTWO) instead of peeking at your 401(k).

Year to date as of Friday's close, the market's performance makes grim reading. The S&P 500 has risen 1%, the Nasdaq Composite COMP has fallen 2.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA was broadly flat, and the Russell 2000 RUT had gained 4%. Keep in mind, the market has been volatile in recent weeks amid shaken confidence in AI-related stocks.

Related: Nvidia's leadership saga unfolds as demand is surging for Anthropic's IPO

Weathering storms

Nvidia is one of the largest components of major stock market indexes, with a market capitalization of $3.75 trillion as of Wednesday afternoon. Its performance is closely watched alongside that of other AI-related stocks, including Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Intel (INTC), Micron Technology (MU), Dell Technologies (DELL) and Oracle (ORCL).

You could regard this as the long-awaited AI bubble bursting (although the AI revolution is likely here to stay). You might see it as an overdue correction. Or you could view the ousting of Huang as CEO of Nvidia as another "monster of the week," a TV trope that mirrors real-life market panics. (Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.)

If that volatility has you looking for safer ground, CD rates are reaching up to 5% if you are prepared to lock up your money for anywhere from six months to five years. CDs are better suited for short-term, safe-haven savings like an emergency fund rather than making up a significant part of your long-term investment plan.

You could choose to view these latest events as another 'monster of the week.'

The stock market has weathered quite a few storms in recent years. The more you check your stocks, however, the more apt you are to fret over the volatility, and the more likely you are to sell based on growing fear, unease, and uncertainty.

The geopolitical backdrop - the unpredictable and frankly confusing war in Iran, Russia's invasion of Ukraine and Trump's on-again, off-again trade war - has made many investors and 401(k) account holders nervous and led to fears of a broader correction.

As you move from your 40s into your 50s and 60s, the share of your portfolio invested in stocks typically shifts to reflect the time you have to recover from a major market correction and to mitigate what's known as sequence-of-returns risk.

That risk is especially critical in the years just before and after retirement. A large market decline early in retirement can severely damage your portfolio far more than a similar decline happening many years later. Ultimately, the right asset allocation will depend on your personal risk tolerance.

Don't miss: 'God works in mysterious ways': I became a Nvidia millionaire playing 'World of Warcraft.' Am I smart - or just lucky?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Buying real estate

Selling shares that you presumably hope will see you through retirement to invest in real estate is a dramatic move. The Florida property market is as good as any to use as an example: The average home value in Florida is approximately $375,000, down 0.5% over the past year, with homes going to "pending" in around 47 days on average, according to Zillow (Z).

As the Moneyist reader points out, the Florida real estate market has fallen and stabilized, with single-family and luxury homes showing resilience. Condos, meanwhile, have had a rougher time due to oversupply and softening demand, compounded by persistently high interest rates and regulatory costs.

Stocks and real estate can both provide passive income, but are you ready to be an absentee landlord and shoulder the costs that come with it because of a bad week or month in the stock market? Good luck with those property taxes and storm insurance premiums.

You are better off playing Grand Theft Auto VI than peeking at your 401(k).

Deals exist in the Sunshine State and elsewhere. Florida's new-build construction market has remained resilient in the face of rising inventory, despite higher rates. Major homebuilders are offering aggressive incentives to buyers who use their in-house lenders. That particular trend is happening nationwide, too.

In November, 46% of homebuilders cut prices, the highest share since COVID-19, according to a monthly survey by the National Association of Home Builders released Tuesday. The average price cut remained steady at 6% for an eighth consecutive month. Meanwhile, 68% of builders offered sales incentives - also a post-COVID high.

For better or for worse - and with AI's help recently - the stock market is a beast that keeps on roaring. Over the last 10 years, the S&P 500 gained more than 230% in value compared to roughly 84% for U.S. residential home prices, analysts say, and that's before factoring in dividends or the costs of owning a home.

If you're considering a big portfolio change today or tomorrow, you need an adviser who can take a long, sober look at your allocations, age, retirement plans and goals, your investing timeline, your mix of U.S. versus overseas stocks, and your holdings in bonds and cash. All that work will take your mind off Nvidia.

Please be careful, my friends, before swapping one volatile asset for another.

Related: 'The thought of living to 100 terrifies me': Is Social Security a giant Ponzi scheme?

data.title: I'm terrified of a market crash. Should I put $400,000 of my $1 million retirement savings into an annuity?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'We have a house worth $450,000. Our combined annual income is $125,000.'

"We don't have any nonqualified brokerage investments, and our combined annual income is $125,000." (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Quentin,

I'm wondering what your thoughts are on putting our house and other assets into a trust. Could it help reduce taxes or protect our assets from lawsuits, bankruptcy or other unforeseen circumstances? If so, what are the potential downsides or pitfalls?

We have a house worth $450,000 and about $1 million in retirement assets held in various qualified accounts. I'd also be interested in your thoughts on annuities for capital preservation and guaranteed income.

Would it make sense to put $400,000 of our $1 million in qualified retirement accounts into an annuity that would begin paying out at age 65, guaranteeing us $40,000 a year for life, while leaving the remaining $600,000 invested in a brokerage account for capital appreciation?

My spouse and I are 55 and 54, respectively. We're both working and plan to continue until 65. We're terrified of a market crash. We don't have any nonqualified brokerage investments, and our combined annual income is $125,000.

Curious in the Midwest

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'Nvidia has me spooked ': Should I sell my stocks or buy real estate?

That money you invest in an annuity is no longer readily available, and you give up any stock-market gains it might have earned.

Dear Curious,

I'll outline the advantages of your proposal - and then move on to the cons.

First, the pros of putting your money in an annuity, I presume, are to find a haven for part of your nest egg, albeit at a potentially lower rate than the stock market could provide. If you moved $400,000 from traditional 401(k)s or IRAs into an IRA annuity, the transaction generally would not trigger income taxes or the 10% early-withdrawal penalty, provided the funds are transferred correctly. A direct trustee-to-trustee transfer is typically the simplest approach. If you were selling $400,000 worth of investments in an ordinary brokerage account, however, you could owe capital-gains taxes on any profits realized from the sale.

Annuities provide guaranteed income, much like Social Security, which you presumably plan to take when you reach full retirement age. What you receive depends on the type of annuity: your initial investment, the interest rate or other terms you lock in and, of course, the payment schedule. Payouts can also vary with your age, your sex and whether the product is a joint-life annuity. If you expect to live a long time, a lifetime annuity can protect you from outliving your retirement savings. The trade-off is access: That money is no longer readily available, and you give up any stock-market gains it might have earned.

Annuities provide guaranteed income, much like Social Security.

An annuity is neither a bond nor cash. It works as an insurance contract: you pay an insurance company in exchange for income. An immediate annuity starts paying within a year of purchase, while a deferred annuity starts at a later date. Money in a 401(k) or IRA that is invested in stocks can grow over time and help keep pace with inflation. Annuity income is usually fixed, so it can lose purchasing power as prices rise unless you add an inflation adjustment or rider, but that protection also comes at a price: a lower initial payout. Annuity fees can be as much as 10% of the value of your contract. Surrender charges can be substantial if you withdraw money early.

But I have some questions: I understand why the prospect of $40,000 in guaranteed annual income is tempting. If payments continued for those periods, you would collect $400,000 over 10 years, $800,000 over 20 years and potentially $1.2 million over 30 years. Make sure you read the fine print. Is that $40,000 guaranteed income for one person's lifetime? Or is it for both of your lifetimes? Does the surviving spouse continue to receive the full $40,000-a-year income? Is there a death benefit or return-of-premium provision or rider if one spouse dies? Last but not least, are the $40,000-a-year payments adjusted for inflation?

Don't miss: My wife and I are in our 70s. Should we pay off our 2.5% mortgage or invest in a stock market driven by AI?

Investing in the stock market

Third, the pros of leaving the money in the stock market: If you left your $400,000 invested for another 10 years instead of putting it into an annuity, it could grow to approximately $592,000 at an annual return of 4%, $787,000 at 7%, or $864,000 at 8%. These estimates assume annual compounding, with investment earnings reinvested, and exclude taxes, fees and additional contributions. The biggest difference between this scenario and the option of buying an annuity with your $400,000 is that the former is not guaranteed. You are potentially giving up the prospect of a larger return in exchange for security.

An annuity and a trust provide different estate-planning functions. Annuities distribute your assets per the terms of the contract, whereas a trust is designed to manage, protect and distribute your estate during your lifetime and beyond. As this guide on Estate Guru points out, trusts and annuities solve different estate-planning problems: (1) Bypassing probate or buying an annuity isn't an estate plan. (2) A trust can manage your assets if you become incapacitated, provide for minor children or beneficiaries with special needs, address the complications of a blended family and set out the conditions for an inheritance.

Revocable living trusts can benefit people with modest estates, particularly those seeking to avoid probate or plan for incapacity. For families with complicated estates, putting accounts and assets under a single trustee can keep everything running smoothly. It can also help prevent conflicts involving beneficiary designations. Marital trusts matter most in blended families, where each spouse wants to be sure their own children are provided for if the other dies. A special-needs trust can supplement government benefits, while a spendthrift trust can prevent beneficiaries from selling or using their future inheritance as collateral for a loan.

Know what you're buying, and be sure you're doing it for the right reasons.

Related: Is Social Security a Ponzi scheme? No. Don't get carried away with 1930s-era prophecies of doom.

data.title: 'Never too late to start': Practical investing advice from some of the top women in finance
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

There are plenty of rich and influential women in the U.S. Their time may be coming.

The message is starting to get out to the next generation of women in finance.

Go to any list of the most influential people in investing and you get names like Warren Buffett, Benjamin Graham, Jack Bogle and Peter Lynch. People study their methods, devour their autobiographies and quote them repeatedly. Women rarely make the cut.

There are rich, influential women in the U.S., and plenty now in high finance and investing. It's just that few have the kind of personality-driven followings that turns them into household names and get them quoted in high-school term papers.

Jenny Harrington and Rebecca Patterson hope that their new book of essays written by some of the most successful women in finance can add these voices to the conversation. "Investment Wisdom for Our Friends and Loved Ones: Timeless Lessons From Today's Top Finance Experts" features advice on how to save, invest and make your way in the world, written as missives to their friends and families. All of the contributors were volunteers and the proceeds go to charity.

Harrington's essay, for instance, was written with the next generation in mind. She got her start on Wall Street at an investing firm - where the recruiters first wanted to steer her into sales because of her gender, but she wanted to go deep on strategy. She worked her way up until she found herself in a toxic work environment and then left to start her own shop, Gilman Hill Asset Management. She has become a frequent contributor on CNBC and one of the top gurus of dividend investing with the book, titled simply, "Dividend Investing."

Her key bit of wisdom: "A lack of investment experience is never a personal failing but rather a reality of life for most people." Her solution for changing that is for people to get educated.

Other contributors include co-editor Patterson, who is currently an independent director at Vanguard; Liz Ann Sonders, chief investment strategist at the Schwab Center for Financial Research; Cate Faddis, senior portfolio manager at Zevin Asset Management; and Susan Kasser, head of Neuberger Berman Private Debt.

Collectively, they counsel prudence, diversification and curiosity. To get started, Bryn Talkington, who founded her own investment firm, Requisite Capital Management, said not to be afraid to just dive in, no matter where you are in your life. "Be comfortable being uncomfortable. You are never too late to start - anything," she wrote.

Jamie Franco, a managing director at investment firm TCW, advocated teamwork. "The myth of the lone-wolf investor with a brilliant hunch is just that: a myth. Sustainable success is a team sport," she said.

Each one tells a little bit of their origin stories, which are not the typical country-club backgrounds you might expect of financial-industry professionals. Many of these women had hardscrabble upbringings that made them appreciate the value of a dollar well before they ever started working with traders where millions of dollars were at stake in mere seconds.

"The way I found my way to money management was that I was a cashier and I liked counting money in the drawer," Harrington said. While her family's fortunes fluctuated, she took an internship at a hedge fund and found her own footing. She attributes this rise through experience to her being able to articulate financial concepts in a way that it's easy to understand.

"Maybe because I didn't start off on third base with investment knowledge - and many of the other contributors, either - now I'm able to speak about it," she said.

That ability to communicate with others is key to getting women onto the canon of investing legends. Warren Buffett would be just another billionaire if he didn't write his regular investing letters that anyone can read, and put out his philosophies in print. Same with the other usual male suspects on the lists, from Benjamin Franklin to Milton Friedman to Jim Cramer.

"They're constantly putting themselves out there and they have these wonderful quips," said Harrington. "They're very profound, but they're also written in a way that just about anyone can understand them. It's that combination of having huge assets but also a very, very big personality."

One thing that hampered women in the investing world, Harrington said, is that many of them work for firms where compliance keeps them under wraps. When you work your way up the ranks today - there weren't many (or any) women at the executive level when Benjamin Graham was coming up - you have to play by corporate rules and that means that every TV appearance, social-media post and book proposal is highly regulated. The system is set up to discourage the quotable - and shareable - witty clip.

Sometimes there's also fear of blowback that holds people back from saying what they think. "I said some innocuous stuff on social media about Nvidia and people are calling me the stupidest person on Earth," said Harrington, who shrugged it off as probably coming from not even a real person.

These constraints actually made it complicated for Harrington and Patterson to get contributions for the book, in some cases. "You see that lack of willingness to just, you know, go hard," Harrington said.

Harrington hopes the book will encourage a new generation of people - not just women - to learn to invest and build their financial knowledge. And that other women in the industry will be inspired to tell their stories and share their wisdom.

"The scales are just so unbalanced. But when they are just a hair more balanced, I'm going to bet you that five books come out of this one," Harrington said.

data.title: 'I felt so seen': Why families across America are laughing - and crying - over SNL's 'Sister' sketch
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

The late-night comedy sketch does the impossible by making female caregivers feel seen

A screenshot from Saturday Night Live's "Sister" comedy sketch.

With all that's been going on in the world in the past week - the Nvidia (NVDA) scandal, the FAA flight stoppage, the Microsoft outage, the midterm election fallout - it's incredible that "Saturday Night Live" had the bandwidth to strike a cultural chord with a sketch about the all-too-real sibling imbalance in caregiving.

More than 2.2 million had watched the official YouTube clip of the late-night comedy institution's "Sister" sketch, featuring host John Mulaney, by noon on Monday, and other links were circulating the web.

"Sister" hit my feed first thing Sunday morning, just as I was about to go on stage at a conference to talk about - you guessed it - caregiving. The merciless impact on women who care for family members is a big part of my talk, which stems from my own experiences of caregiving and the book I wrote about it, called "My Mother's Money."

It's more than just the emotional toll, but also the out-of-pocket costs - which AARP now pegs at an average of $11,500 per year - long-term career costs, dented retirement savings and lower Social Security benefits. Mulaney jokes that if you text "dad fell," your sister will quit her job, break her lease and fly across the country to step into the breach. So true.

I felt seen. Everyone in my orbit felt seen.

"So sad, and so true," said Nancy Brenner, a writer and content strategist in New York who has been caring for her mother for years.

Kim Elliott, who founded a newsletter for caregivers called "Gray Monster" - which has the tag line that they're there to help "because we know your brother won't" - heard from more than 100 of her subscribers over the weekend. She thought the skit resonated so much because it was so true. "The punchline is that 'Sister' is free. And she is, to everyone but herself," said Elliot.

"That's the 'daughter tax,'" said Lily Vittayarukskul, founder of WaterLily, a company that helps families connect with long-term-care policies. "When families don't plan for the cost of care, they can end up paying for it with a daughter's financial future."

Feeling seen is a big deal. Caregiving is invisible labor, and the people who do it also feel invisible. I saw this repeatedly over the weekend when talking to various clusters of people at the Bogleheads conference, which focuses on financial education for do-it-yourself investors who follow the model set by Vanguard founder Jack Bogle. People just wanted to talk. They had fear in their eyes. Many were deep in a care situation for an aging parent, and also were seeing the train coming straight for them. Some were worried about their children.

There were plenty of men in these conversations, all just as concerned and involved as the women I met. Caregiving is a lot for anyone. But there is statistical truth in the view that it hits women harder than men; between 60% and 70% of family caregivers these days are women, depending on which survey you pick. And this represents a lot of progress: It used to be closer to 100% women, but go back more than 30 or 40 years and it was just expected, not measured.

"I laughed at 'Sister,' and then I winced, because I've met that brother more than once," said David Goodman, co-founder of CompassCare, which coordinates care for families when neither brother or sister can be there 24/7. "Look at how far parenting has come. A generation ago, paternity leave barely existed and nobody expected a dad at the pediatrician's office. Today, both are normal. Caregiving for aging parents is on the same path, just a few decades behind. Right now, it falls disproportionately on women. It can and should be shared, and that shift is already under way."

But we're not quite there yet. At one point over the weekend, I found myself talking to a table full of men about caregiving. One asked me if I had siblings who helped me on my caregiving journey.

I looked around and said, "Oh, I don't think my usual joke about this is going to land with this group." He said try it. I said, "I have an older brother."

At a table full of women, we'd all have a good laugh about this, because we know that it means just what the SNL skit lays out in dark humor: You get a call and drop everything, while your proverbial brother goes on with his life. But the men at the table just blinked.

I asked the original questioner if he had siblings. He said he had two sisters; they were closer to their parents, and that's why they ended up doing more. Of course, I nodded. He then asked the right follow-up question: "What could I do better to help?"

I said that the No. 1 complaint I hear from female caregivers about their siblings, no matter the gender, is that they second-guess and criticize, but never step in to do the work. It's incredibly frustrating to be buried under the weight of caregiving and then have somebody from the outside telling you that you are doing it wrong. (See also: Jennifer Grey's Home Instead commercial reprising her "Ferris Bueller" character.) So the best thing a sibling on the sidelines can do is call to ask how the caregiver is doing, and offer love and support instead of potshots.

Maybe that's the big takeaway that the SNL "Sister" moment will have. With the clip being passed from sibling to sibling - one poster on social media said she group-texted the clip to her sisters and excluded her brother, but added that others might want their brothers to see it - it will spark some "aha!" moments and some loving conversations.

I can already imagine the one happening in the Seidell family, after SNL writer Streeter Seidell posted that he dedicated the piece, which he co-wrote with Mikey Day and Simon Rich (with an assist from Chase Rosenberg), to his sister Heidi.

"Family caregivers rarely see their lives reflected in pop culture. Caregiving is an incredibly serious subject, but sometimes levity is the best entry point into a difficult conversation. I'm grateful to SNL for opening that door," said Gray Monster's Elliot.

Or, perhaps, you can dream bigger. Ai-jen Poo, who has dedicated her whole career to being an advocate for caregivers, posted this: "Here's the quiet part: it doesn't have to be this way...this dynamic is the result of avoidable policy choices...that we can change!"

data.title: America is definitely rich enough to fix Social Security and Medicare. Here's how.
data.description:
By Brett Arends

This one, simple, low-pain tax solves all the problems

Pay 1% a year? Moi?

To hear many people tell it, America's looming fiscal crises can't be fixed without enormous pain or costs - if it at all.

The country's national debt just hit $40 trillion, equal to about 100% of annual gross domestic product. Social Security's trust fund is due to run out of money in 2032 (or 2034 at the latest), and without some radical fix, benefits would have to be slashed by about a fifth. Medicare's Part A (hospital insurance) trust fund is due to run out of money around the same time. The trust fund for Medicare Part B (medical insurance) doesn't even have any money; it is funded by general tax revenues.

Any look at the long-term numbers seems terrifying: Trillions of dollars in deficits and unfunded liabilities, stretching as far as the eye can see.

Some say we will need to slash retirement benefits for future retirees, and drop millions from Medicaid (the latter is actually happening; it was part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, along with tax cuts). Others talk about hefty income-tax hikes - for example, by abolishing the cap on the incomes subject to Social Security payroll taxes, which would effectively add an extra 12.4% tax on all income over $192,300 (in 2027).

Others offer big "wealth" taxes applied to the rich, the super-rich or the super-duper-rich. California voters just rejected a one-off 5% wealth tax on billionaires, but only after billionaires spent a fortune to defeat the measure. And the vote was pretty close.

But all of this is wrong. It is based on old-fashioned, outdated, backward-looking and increasingly irrelevant thinking, which is about as un-American as anything could be. It would be as if the U.S. government in the past had been supported by, say, a tax on buggy-whip sales, and as buggy whips passed into history, the revenues dried up, and the politicians and voters stood around, baffled, saying: "Well, we're screwed - there's nothing else we can do."

To cut to the chase: While American incomes have been struggling, especially for the middle class and especially compared with inflation, American wealth has not. The people of this country, in aggregate, are richer than they have ever been before. They are richer than any group of people in history, by multiple orders of magnitude. Croesus, the ancient benchmark of richness, had nothing on 2026 America.

As of the last count, the total assets in private hands came out to $217 trillion. That figure has doubled in just 10 years, and risen by a third in the last five years alone. Even adjusted for inflation, Americans in total have twice as much wealth as they did in 2000, at the tail end of the 1990s boom - a time generally looked back upon now as one of broad prosperity (and also one when the federal budget was actually in surplus). There is twice as much wealth now.

These figures come from the Federal Reserve, which conducts the most exhaustive and authoritative analysis every quarter. These numbers only relate to households and various nonprofits (we're looking at you, Harvard and Yale endowments). They don't even include wealth held by the government and the states - such as all the land and property, the gold in Fort Knox, and so on. Nor do they include all the private wealth held in the form of collectibles, whether they be gold coins, jewelry, $800,000 bottles of wine, $70 million vintage automobiles, $190 million Van Gogh paintings, and the like. The total wealth has risen $22 trillion just in the past 12 months.

A simple, flat, low 1% annual tax on all assets would generate $2.2 trillion in annual revenue, with far less pain or economic distortion than any other alternative - whether it be income taxes, corporation taxes, import taxes (aka tariffs) or sales taxes.

That one tax would be enough to plug the entire federal deficit - which totaled $2 trillion in the fiscal year just ended - and put the federal budget in surplus. Combined with even some modest entitlement reform, such as capping payments for the wealthiest retirees, it would transform the entire picture from gloom to boom with a stroke.

An asset tax doesn't need to be purely additive; it could replace some other taxes. As budgets do not need to be in surplus over time, this tax might actually create some room to cut other taxes, such as middle-class income taxes.

This is not the same as a "wealth tax." First, it's a low tax rate of just 1% a year. Wealth taxes are typically much higher, and often punitive. Second, it would apply to everyone, not just the rich. And it would be a tax on assets, not net worth.

One of the remarkable things about such a tax is that it would simultaneously be flat, which conservatives love, and highly progressive, which liberals love. The reason for that is because the distribution of wealth in this country is so insanely uneven that one family in 100 owns a third of all U.S. wealth. The poorest 50% in total own 2.3%. (You don't have to be a communist to think that's insane and no way to run a country.)

The richest 0.1%, meaning one family in 1,000, owns about 15% of all the wealth, or six times as much as the poorest 50%.

A simple, flat asset tax would also be far easier to collect - and involve far less IRS intrusion into our lives and far less paperwork - than any other. Almost all of that wealth is held in stocks, bonds, mutual funds, pension-fund assets, hedge funds, cash, money-market accounts and the like, according to Federal Reserve data. The value of these things are already tracked either annually (in the case of real estate), quarterly or - in the case of your stock portfolio - by the minute. Private businesses and consumer durables, probably the only things difficult to value, in aggregate make up about 12% of the total.

At a Senate hearing on Wednesday, Republican Sen. Rick Scott of Florida raised a straw-man argument by asking a witness what would happen if the U.S. government confiscated all the wealth owned by billionaires to finance Social Security and Medicare.

Such an obviously ridiculous proposition is used to scare people, especially those addicted to certain TV channels. No serious person has suggested or is contemplating anything so absurd. But a 1% tax a year on all wealth would constitute only a fraction of the annual return that most assets earn.

(It's always exciting to hear from Sen. Scott, especially when it comes to the soaring cost of entitlements, because he - or rather, the healthcare company where he was CEO, Columbia/HCA (HCA) - held the all-time record for the biggest fraud ever committed against Medicare. It ended up paying $1.7 billion in fines, damages and penalties. Scott himself was never charged with criminal conduct, although a cynic might ask that if he didn't know what was going on at the company, why was he being paid millions of dollars a year as CEO?)

Virginia Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, a leading moderate, pointed out during the same debate that the nature of the economy had changed. More and more people are living on wealth, instead of just income, so maybe the tax code needs to change in response. He was talking about taxes on capital gains and investment income, but the same principle applies to assets overall.

Sen. Warner made his fortune in the private sector, from a standing start, before going into politics, so he may know something about wealth creation. We need more people like that in politics - and more people willing to be honest about the gigantic accumulation of wealth in the U.S., and what we can afford.

-Brett Arends
